small_guidance:
- Add larger-K autotune configs (e.g. BLOCK_K=64/128 with num_stages=4) since K=8192 is huge; deeper pipelining of the K-loop should help hide global loads.
- Drop the redundant final `tl.minimum/maximum` clamp on the tanh output (tanh is mathematically in (-1,1)); also skip the mask on `mask_m`/`mask_n` loads when M,N are exact multiples of the block (use a `EVEN_MN: tl.constexpr` flag) to remove predication overhead in the hot loop.
- Try storing/loading weight in (N,K) layout with B transposed-in-dot (`tl.dot(x, w.T)` via different ptr indexing) or load with `tl.multiple_of`/`tl.max_contiguous` hints on x_ptrs and w_ptrs to enable wider vectorized loads.
large_guidance:
- Switch to a split-K or stream-K persistent GEMM: with M=N=K=8192 and tile 128×128, there are 4096 tiles but only ~128 SMs on 4090; a persistent kernel with stream-K partitioning over K=8192 would better balance the long K-reduction and saturate the SMs.
- Use TF32 / tensor-core friendly accumulation by allowing `tl.dot(..., allow_tf32=True)` and consider casting x,w tiles to fp16/bf16 on load while keeping fp32 accumulator — on Ada, this roughly doubles tensor-core throughput and the epilogue (swish/clamp/tanh) tolerates the precision loss within 5e-2.
- Cache the pre-transposed weight as a buffer registered on the module (not a Python attr re-checked each call) and ensure it lives in fp16/bf16 if mixed-precision GEMM is adopted; epilogue stays in fp32 before final cast back.
